newsitem.title: FRANCE: Colombia seeks to join money-laundering accord.
newsitem.headline: Colombia seeks to join money-laundering accord.

text.p: Colombia wants to join a European convention on money laundering to fight drug-trafficking after passing a landmark law to seize multibillion-dollar assets from drug lords, Foreign Minister Emma Maria Mejia said on Wednesday.

Mejia, visiting Paris on her way to Washington, said Colombia had applied previously to join the 1990 convention on laundering, tracing and seizing the proceeds of crime, but its legislation had so far fallen short of the requirements.
"We are greatly interested in joining as we believe this is an adequate mechanism," she told Reuters in an interview.

Mejia said Bogota believed that a multilateral fight against drug-trafficking would give better results than the bilateral U.S. approach in decertifying Colombia as a partner in its anti-drug war and threatening trade sanctions next year.

Mejia said the new law to seize the illicit gains made by the drug barons over the past 20 years, which she said ran into billions of dollars, had given the world strong evidence of Colombia's determination to fight drugs.
New Colombian Vice-President Carlos Lemos Simmonds has said the law, passed by parliament last week, should make the United States rethink its policy towards Bogota.

Mejia discussed the drugs fight with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette on Tuesday, but was not expecting to raise it during her working visit to Washington starting on Thursday which would focus on trade, energy and environmental issues.

The United States last March disqualified Colombia as an ally in the war on drugs, saying the cartels had corrupted every level of the state. It revoked the visa of President Ernesto Samper after he refused to extradite four Cali cartel leaders.
Washington argued that Samper had accepted money from drug lords to finance his 1994 presidential campaign. The Colombian Congress cleared Samper of the charges in June.

Mejia, who had talks with Cuban President Fidel Castro in Havana last week during a meeting of Caribbean countries, denied reports that he or Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina could mediate the release of 60 Colombian army conscripts held by Marxist guerrillas for three months.
"On the contrary, they said they were confident that Colombia could solve its problems domestically," she said.
Castro had been widely credited last June for winning the release of former Colombian President Cesar Gaviria's brother from another leftist group of kidnappers.
Mejia said she also discussed the kidnapping of the conscripts, a highly emotional issue at home, with several of the 25 foreign ministers attending the Havana meeting.
Samper has said mediation efforts were being carried out by the Red Cross.

The soldiers were seized on August 30 by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and another 27 were killed in the attack which marked the start of one of the bloodiest guerrilla offensives in three decades of armed uprising.

Mejia said 25 abducted foreign technicians, including a French engineer, were in the hands of guerrillas who had turned kidnappings, robberies and links with drug traffickers into a lucrative business yielding half a billion dollars annually.
Despite the danger faced by foreigners working in remote places, the kidnappings had not yet affected investment or the despatching of expatriates to Colombia, she said.
